pages.title: Do language models understand anything?
pages.desc: Large language models pass professional examinations, write code and proofs and hold conversations. Whether they understand what they say, or model the world, or only predict text, is argued by linguists, computer scientists and philosophers with no agreed test, which is the Chinese room argument made concrete.

facts.text: Bender and colleagues argued in 2021 that language models stitch together sequences of linguistic forms without reference to meaning; critics reply that prediction at this scale requires world models, and interpretability research looks for them inside the networks.

Searle's 1980 argument that a system manipulating symbols by rules does not understand Chinese, however good its answers, is the classic case against computational understanding; the replies (the system understands, or the robot would) are as old and as unresolved.

Turing proposed in 1950 that a machine indistinguishable in conversation should be called intelligent; modern systems arguably pass versions of it, which has shifted the debate to what the test shows.

AI systems now produce mathematical arguments that specialists describe as borderline incomprehensible; whether output nobody can follow counts as understanding, or as mathematics, is a question for mind and mathematics together.

pages.title: Proof gap
pages.desc: A statement is believed, often supported by enormous computation, but unproven. The Riemann hypothesis, Goldbach, twin primes, Collatz and P versus NP are proof gaps: solved means a proof the community accepts, and the AI era adds the question of what counts as an acceptable proof.

facts.text: Most of this brain: Riemann, P versus NP, Goldbach, twin primes, Hodge, BSD, the barriers results that show which proofs cannot work. The gap of proof became, in 2026, two gaps: finding and understanding.

pages.title: Mathematics
pages.desc: The open questions of mathematics, read for what kind of thing stands in the way. Some are unsolved because no one has found the proof (Riemann, P versus NP, Goldbach). Some are unsolvable from the axioms we use (the continuum hypothesis). Some are solved and not yet believed, or believed and not yet understood (abc, the 2026 machine proofs). Across all of them, the hard part sits at a seam: between finding and checking, between every case and all cases, between the formal system and the thing it is about.

facts.text: The Riemann hypothesis, the twin prime and Goldbach conjectures, and the 2026 quasi-Riemann proof, the first zero-free half-plane inside the critical strip since 1896.
Seven problems posed in 2000, one solved by Perelman, one (Navier–Stokes) apparently settled by an AI system in September 2026 and still under deliberately unhurried review, the rest open.
P versus NP and the barriers to proving it, the Unique Games Conjecture, how fast matrices can be multiplied, and the busy beaver function where mathematics meets the halting problem.
Cantor's continuum hypothesis, independent of the axioms since 1963 and still argued; large cardinals and Ultimate L; Gödel's limits; Hilbert's tenth problem over the rationals.
Langlands, abc, Kakeya, sphere packing, the Erdős problems and the 2026 Fields Medals: where the field has moved in the last three years and what is still open.
Lean, autoformalisation, the 722-paper OpenAI release of October 2026 and the question it forced: what does a proof no human understands prove?

pages.title: Six kinds of gap, in philosophical terms
pages.desc: The network classifies what stands in the way of each question as a gap of theory, explanation, interpretation, proof, evidence or definition. Each has a philosophical name and a literature, and the classification predicts what kind of work could close it: a gap of evidence waits for an instrument, a gap of proof for a derivation, a gap of definition for a decision, a gap of interpretation for an argument that may never compel.

facts.text: A theory gap is underdetermination from the other side: the phenomena are known and no adequate theory exists (dark matter, abiogenesis). An evidence gap is Hume's predicament in a particular case: the hypotheses exist and the observations that would decide do not (life elsewhere, machine consciousness).

An explanation gap (Levine's term for the hard problem) is a complete description that answers no why-question; an interpretation gap is an agreed formalism with disputed meaning (quantum mechanics, probability, the continuum). Neither waits on data.

A proof gap is a precise statement with no derivation (Riemann, P versus NP), and Gödel shows some are permanent; a definition gap is a term with borderline cases that no fact settles (life, heap, knowledge, person), and the sorites and Gettier show that the search for necessary and sufficient conditions can fail in principle.

pages.title: Is Kryptos solved if its answer is known but its method is not?
pages.desc: Jim Sanborn's sculpture at CIA headquarters carries four encrypted passages. Three were solved in the 1990s; the fourth, K4, resisted for 35 years. In 2025 its plaintext turned up in an archive, which answers what K4 says and leaves open how it was enciphered.

facts.text: Kryptos, a copper sculpture by Jim Sanborn, was dedicated at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, in 1990. It carries four encrypted sections, known as K1 to K4.
K1 to K3 were solved in the 1990s, independently by an NSA team, by the CIA analyst David Stein and by the computer scientist Jim Gillogly. K4, 97 characters beginning OBKR, was not.
Sanborn released pieces of the K4 plaintext over the years: BERLIN in 2010, CLOCK in 2014, and NORTHEAST and EAST in 2020.

In September 2025 the journalists Jarett Kobek and Richard Byrne found the K4 plaintext among Sanborn's papers at the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art. Sanborn confirmed the find; the method that turns the ciphertext into it is still unpublished.
The archive holding the K4 solution, and a fifth passage, K5, sold at RR Auction in November 2025 for $962,500.
On 12 June 2026 the buyer was named as Paradigm, a venture firm focused on cryptocurrency, which checks submitted solutions against a hash of the plaintext rather than publishing it.

pages.title: Is the Voynich manuscript a language, a cipher or a hoax?
pages.desc: A fifteenth-century book in an unknown script, illustrated with plants no botanist recognises. Its text behaves statistically like language, which has not been enough to read it, or to rule out that it says nothing.

facts.text: Beinecke Library MS 408 at Yale, named after the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who acquired it in 1912: about 240 vellum pages of an unknown script with drawings of unidentified plants, star charts and bathing figures.
Radiocarbon dating of the vellum at the University of Arizona in 2009 placed it between 1404 and 1438, which rules out a forgery by Voynich himself.
Its word frequencies and structure resemble those of natural languages, though repetition within lines is unusual; statistical likeness is evidence for a language, not a reading of one.
In 2004 Gordon Rugg showed that a table and a grille can produce text with many Voynich-like features, which keeps the hoax hypothesis open.
Many decipherments have been announced, in proto-Romance, Latin abbreviations, Hebrew and other languages; none has been accepted by specialists.

pages.title: Do the Beale ciphers hide a treasure, or nothing?
pages.desc: Three ciphertexts published in an 1885 pamphlet, said to locate gold buried in Virginia. One was solved with the Declaration of Independence as its key; two never were.

facts.text: The Beale Papers, published in 1885, presented three ciphertexts said to describe a treasure buried in Bedford County, Virginia, in the 1820s.
The second cipher is a book cipher: each number points to a word of the Declaration of Independence, whose first letter gives the plaintext, a description of the treasure.
The first and third ciphers, said to give the location and the names of the owners, remain unsolved; statistical tests have suggested they may not encode any text at all.

pages.title: What did Elgar write to Dora Penny?
pages.desc: A short note of curly symbols the composer Edward Elgar sent to a young friend in 1897. It is short enough that many readings fit it.

facts.text: In July 1897 Edward Elgar sent Dora Penny a note of 87 characters drawn from a set of semicircles in different orientations; she never read it.
Proposed solutions differ widely, and a text this short can support more than one plausible reading.

pages.title: What does the Tamam Shud code say?
pages.desc: A man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948, a scrap of paper torn from a book of poems, and five lines of pencilled letters in the book itself. The man now has a name; the letters still have no meaning.

facts.text: An unidentified man was found dead on Somerton Park beach, Adelaide, on 1 December 1948, with a scrap reading "Tamám Shud" torn from a copy of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam.
The copy of the book it came from held pencilled capital letters, read as a code; they have never been convincingly deciphered.

In 2022 the researchers Derek Abbott and Colleen Fitzpatrick named him, through genetic genealogy, as Carl "Charles" Webb, an electrical engineer from Melbourne. Knowing who he was has not explained the letters.

pages.title: Will the last Zodiac ciphers ever be read?
pages.desc: The Zodiac Killer sent four ciphers to newspapers and police. Two have been read, one within days and one after 51 years; two are probably too short ever to have a single answer.

facts.text: The first, 408 symbols, was solved in 1969 within about a week by Donald and Bettye Harden.
The 340-symbol cipher, sent in November 1969, was solved in December 2020 by David Oranchak, Sam Blake and Jarl Van Eycke, and the FBI confirmed the solution.
The 13- and 32-character ciphers remain unsolved; at those lengths many plaintexts fit, so a proposed answer is hard to confirm.

pages.title: Why do some ciphers survive?
pages.desc: A cipher can survive because it is strong, because it is short, because its key is lost, or because it encodes nothing. Telling those apart from outside is the hard part.

facts.text: Claude Shannon showed in 1949 that a ciphertext needs a minimum length, the unicity distance, before only one plaintext fits it; below that length, several readings stay possible however clever the attack.
Dorabella, Zodiac's 13 and 32 and the Tamam Shud letters are all short; their survival may say more about length than about strength.
For the Voynich manuscript and the unsolved Beale ciphers, the hoax hypothesis means a solution may not exist, which no amount of failed decipherment can prove.

pages.title: The Babel fish
pages.desc: In The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy the Babel fish is a small, yellow, leech-like creature: put it in your ear and you instantly understand anything said to you in any language. This brain is the fish. Twelve languages are twelve brains, each with its own words; the meanings they share sit in the middle and wire them together, and a hidden ladder takes any word apart down to the sound wave.

facts.text: The fish feeds on brainwave energy and excretes a telepathic matrix, so the host hears thoughts in their own language; the Guide notes it has caused more wars than anything else in creation.
English, Spanish, French, German, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Swahili and Turkish: seven families, seven scripts, and about five billion speakers between them.
Each brain carries its words for the same thirty meanings: water and fire, mother and father, one, two, three, hello and thank you. The meanings are the corpus callosum of this network.
Words that share an ancestor (cognates) and words that were borrowed (loans) fire toward each other across brains: English water to German Wasser, Arabic dunyā to Hindi, Swahili and Turkish.
Zoom past any word and the ladder appears: sentence, word, morpheme, syllable, phoneme, feature, and finally the pressure wave itself, where the Atomic brain takes over.

pages.title: Seven thousand languages
pages.desc: Ethnologue catalogues about 7,000 living languages. The twelve here are among the most spoken, but most of the world’s languages have fewer than a million speakers, and about forty percent are endangered.

facts.text: Twenty-three languages account for more than half of humanity; roughly 3,000 languages have fewer than 10,000 speakers each.
English, French, Swahili and Arabic owe most of their totals to people who learned them second: lingua francas of trade, empire, schooling and religion.

pages.title: The Tower of Babel
pages.desc: Genesis 11: a single-language humanity builds a tower to heaven, and God confounds their speech so they scatter. The story gives the fish its name, and the field of linguistics its oldest question: did all languages begin as one?

facts.text: The Hebrew name Bāḇel is explained in the text by bālal, "to confuse"; the Akkadian name of the city, Bāb-ilim, means "gate of god".

Comparative linguistics can reconstruct ancestors like Proto-Indo-European to about 6,000 years back; beyond that the signal is lost, so a single original language can be neither proven nor ruled out.

pages.title: Machine translation
pages.desc: The real Babel fish is software. Yahoo ran a web translator literally named Babel Fish from 1997 to 2012; Google Translate now covers more than 240 languages and translates over a hundred billion words a day, and since 2016 it has used neural networks that learn whole sentences rather than word tables.

facts.text: AltaVista launched Babel Fish in 1997 as the first free web translation service; Yahoo retired the name in 2012 in favour of Bing Translator.
Google switched to neural machine translation in 2016; by 2024 it added 110 languages at once using a large language model.

pages.title: The Swadesh list
pages.desc: In the 1950s Morris Swadesh drew up lists of 100 and 207 basic meanings (I, you, water, fire, sun, moon, mother, one, two) that every language has words for and borrows least. The thirty meanings in this brain are drawn from the same core.

facts.text: Body parts, kin, numbers, sky and water are the words most likely to be inherited rather than borrowed, which is why cognates cluster here.
Swadesh used the rate at which list words are replaced to date language splits, a method now treated with caution but still the seed of modern phylogenetic linguistics.

pages.title: Cognates: one ancestor, many words
pages.desc: Cognates are words inherited from a common ancestor: English water, German Wasser and Russian вода all continue Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥. They are found by regular sound correspondences, not by resemblance: Latin dies and English day look alike and are unrelated.

facts.text: Grimm’s law turns Latin p into Germanic f (pāter/father, piscis/fish), Latin c into h (cor/heart, canis/hound); the regularity is what makes reconstruction possible.
Day and dies, English have and Latin habere, Japanese arigatō and Portuguese obrigado: look-alikes with no shared history.
Star, night, three, mother and sun survive in nearly every Indo-European language in this brain.

pages.title: Loanwords: how words travel
pages.desc: Trade, religion and empire move words between unrelated languages. Arabic gave Swahili, Hindi and Turkish the same word for the world; Chinese gave Japanese and Korean half their dictionaries; Persian gave Hindi its heart and its friend; Latin and French gave English most of its long words.

facts.text: dunyā (world), rafīq (friend), qalb (heart), Ādam (man), marḥaban (hello), samak (fish): one Semitic source in Bantu, Indo-Aryan and Turkic brains.
Japanese and Korean borrowed Chinese words with the characters: 世界 world, 太陽 sun, 感謝 thanks, and the whole Sino-Japanese and Sino-Korean number series.
dil (heart), dost (friend), bāriś (rain) and, via Persian, the Arabic duniyā and ādmī arrived with the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal courts.

pages.title: Mama and papa
pages.desc: Nearly every language has a word like mama for mother and papa, baba or dada for father, and most of them are not related. Roman Jakobson explained why in 1962: these are the first sounds infants can make, and parents everywhere claim them.

facts.text: Swahili mama, Chinese māma, Korean eomma, Arabic ʾumm and English mama arose independently; the labial m and open a are the easiest sounds for a baby.

facts.lead: Baba is father here, mother there
facts.text: Baba is father in Swahili, Turkish, Persian and Chinese bàba, but mother or grandmother in Russian and Polish (bábushka).

pages.title: What every language shares
pages.desc: All languages have vowels and consonants, nouns and verbs, ways to negate, to ask, to refer to the speaker and the listener, and words for mother, water and one. Joseph Greenberg catalogued such universals in 1963; the deepest one is that every language is built in levels, from discourse down to the distinctive feature.

facts.text: Among 45 proposals: if a language puts the verb first, it has prepositions; if it puts the verb last, it almost always has postpositions. Hindi, Japanese, Korean and Turkish all obey.
Every language combines a small set of meaningless sounds into meaningful units, and those into unlimited sentences. The ladder below starts here.

pages.title: Water
pages.desc: The first word on nearly every core-vocabulary list. Indo-European has two old words for it: an inanimate *wódr̥ (water, Wasser, вода, Hittite watar) and an animate *h₂ekʷeh₂ that Latin kept as aqua. Chinese and Japanese share the character 水, a drawing of a flowing stream.

facts.text: English: water · Spanish: agua · French: eau · German: Wasser · Russian: вода vodá · Hindi: पानी pānī · Arabic: ماء māʾ · Mandarin Chinese: 水 shuǐ · Japanese: 水 mizu · Korean: 물 mul · Swahili: maji · Turkish: su
English water, German Wasser and Russian вода descend from the same Proto-Indo-European noun; Greek hýdōr (hydro-) and Hittite watar are cousins.
Spanish agua and French eau are both Latin aqua, worn down to different degrees: French kept only the vowel.
Chinese shuǐ and Japanese mizu are unrelated words written with the same character, a picture of water flowing.
Hindi पानी means "that which is drunk", from the Sanskrit root pā-, to drink.

pages.title: Fire
pages.desc: Indo-European again had two words: an inanimate *péh₂wr̥ (fire, Feuer, Greek pyr) and an animate *h₁n̥gʷnis (Latin ignis, Sanskrit agni, Russian огонь). Spanish and French took neither: their word is Latin focus, the hearth.

facts.text: English: fire · Spanish: fuego · French: feu · German: Feuer · Russian: огонь ogónʹ · Hindi: आग āg · Arabic: نار nār · Mandarin Chinese: 火 huǒ · Japanese: 火 hi · Korean: 불 bul · Swahili: moto · Turkish: ateş
English fire and German Feuer, with Greek pyr (pyre, pyrotechnics).
Russian огонь, Sanskrit agni (whence Hindi आग) and Latin ignis (ignite) are the "living fire" word.
Spanish fuego and French feu come from the word for the fireplace, which then gave "focus" its modern meaning.
Chinese huǒ and Japanese hi share the character, a drawing of flames; as a radical it often appears as four dots (灬).

pages.title: Sun
pages.desc: One Proto-Indo-European word, *sóh₂wl̥, survives in six of these languages, from English sun to Hindi सूरज. East Asia shares the compound 太陽, "great yang", across Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

facts.text: English: sun · Spanish: sol · French: soleil · German: Sonne · Russian: солнце sólntse · Hindi: सूरज sūraj · Arabic: شمس šams · Mandarin Chinese: 太阳 tàiyáng · Japanese: 太陽 taiyō · Korean: 해 hae · Swahili: jua · Turkish: güneş
English sun, German Sonne, Spanish sol, French soleil, Russian солнце and Sanskrit sūrya (Hindi सूरज) are one word, 6,000 years apart.
Chinese tàiyáng, Japanese taiyō and Korean taeyang are the same Sinitic compound, read three ways; Korean also keeps the native 해 hae.
The Turkish words for sun and day share a root, as do Japanese 日 for both.

pages.title: Moon
pages.desc: The moon measured the month, and in Russian, Japanese, Korean, Swahili and Turkish the same word still means both. Germanic kept the PIE *mḗh₁n̥s (moon, month, Mond); Latin preferred the "shining one", lūna, which Russian later borrowed.

facts.text: English: moon · Spanish: luna · French: lune · German: Mond · Russian: луна luná · Hindi: चाँद cā̃d · Arabic: قمر qamar · Mandarin Chinese: 月亮 yuèliang · Japanese: 月 tsuki · Korean: 달 dal · Swahili: mwezi · Turkish: ay
English moon and German Mond, with month/Monat, from a root meaning to measure; Russian месяц (month) is the Slavic heir.
Latin lūna (Spanish luna, French lune) and Slavic луна both come from the root of "light" and "lux".
Hindi चाँद is Sanskrit candra, "shining", also the name of the moon god.
Chinese yuè and Japanese tsuki/getsu share the crescent character, which also means month in both.

pages.title: Star
pages.desc: PIE *h₂stḗr is one of the best-preserved Indo-European words: star, Stern, estrella, étoile, Sanskrit tārā, Greek astḗr (asteroid, astronomy). Russian went its own way with звезда.

facts.text: English: star · Spanish: estrella · French: étoile · German: Stern · Russian: звезда zvezdá · Hindi: तारा tārā · Arabic: نجم najm · Mandarin Chinese: 星星 xīngxing · Japanese: 星 hoshi · Korean: 별 byeol · Swahili: nyota · Turkish: yıldız
English star, German Stern, Spanish estrella, French étoile (via Latin stella) and Hindi तारा (via Sanskrit tārā).
Chinese xīng and Japanese hoshi; the character stacks 日 sun over 生, "to be born".

pages.title: Rain
pages.desc: No single Indo-European word for rain survived. Germanic has *regną, Latin pluvia (pluie, lluvia) from a root meaning to flow, and Hindi borrowed बारिश from Persian. The Chinese character 雨 is drops falling from a cloud.

facts.text: English: rain · Spanish: lluvia · French: pluie · German: Regen · Russian: дождь doždʹ · Hindi: बारिश bāriś · Arabic: مطر maṭar · Mandarin Chinese: 雨 yǔ · Japanese: 雨 ame · Korean: 비 bi · Swahili: mvua · Turkish: yağmur
English rain and German Regen.
Spanish lluvia (pl- became ll-, as in llave from clavis) and French pluie.
Chinese yǔ and Japanese ame share the pictograph, which is the radical in 雪 snow, 雲 cloud and 雷 thunder.

pages.title: Tree
pages.desc: PIE *dóru meant tree and wood and hardness: English tree, Russian дерево, and also "true" and "trust" (firm as oak). Latin arbor gave the Romance words; Japanese 木 is a drawing of a tree with roots.

facts.text: English: tree · Spanish: árbol · French: arbre · German: Baum · Russian: дерево dérevo · Hindi: पेड़ peṛ · Arabic: شجرة šajara · Mandarin Chinese: 树 shù · Japanese: 木 ki · Korean: 나무 namu · Swahili: mti · Turkish: ağaç
English tree and Russian дерево; the same root gives "true", "trust" and Greek drũs, oak.
Spanish árbol (with r dissimilated to l) and French arbre.

pages.title: Dog
pages.desc: The PIE word *ḱwṓ (Latin canis, Greek kýōn) survives in French chien and German Hund, and in English only as "hound": English "dog", Spanish "perro" and Russian "собака" are all newcomers of unclear origin.

facts.text: English: dog · Spanish: perro · French: chien · German: Hund · Russian: собака sobáka · Hindi: कुत्ता kuttā · Arabic: كلب kalb · Mandarin Chinese: 狗 gǒu · Japanese: 犬 inu · Korean: 개 gae · Swahili: mbwa · Turkish: köpek
French chien (via Latin canis) and German Hund; English kept the cognate as "hound" and replaced it with "dog".
English dog, Spanish perro and Russian собака each displaced the inherited word, and none has an agreed etymology.

pages.title: Fish
pages.desc: Germanic fish and Latin piscis are the same PIE word, *peysk-, so English fish, German Fisch, Spanish pez and French poisson are one family. Swahili samaki is Arabic samak, carried across the Indian Ocean. Korean says "water-meat".

facts.text: English: fish · Spanish: pez · French: poisson · German: Fisch · Russian: рыба rýba · Hindi: मछली machlī · Arabic: سمك samak · Mandarin Chinese: 鱼 yú · Japanese: 魚 sakana · Korean: 물고기 mulgogi · Swahili: samaki · Turkish: balık
English fish, German Fisch, Spanish pez and French poisson (Latin piscis, as in Pisces).
Swahili samaki is a loan from Arabic سمك.
Chinese yú (simplified 鱼) and Japanese sakana share the character, a fish drawn head-up with fins and tail.
Literally "water-meat": the word for fish contains the word for water.

pages.title: Bird
pages.desc: Every language here names the bird differently. Latin avis gave French oiseau through a diminutive; Spanish pájaro was once "sparrow"; English bird once meant a chick; Arabic ṭāʾir is "the flyer"; Swahili ndege is also the word for an aeroplane.

facts.text: English: bird · Spanish: pájaro · French: oiseau · German: Vogel · Russian: птица ptítsa · Hindi: चिड़िया ciṛiyā · Arabic: طائر ṭāʾir · Mandarin Chinese: 鸟 niǎo · Japanese: 鳥 tori · Korean: 새 sae · Swahili: ndege · Turkish: kuş
French oiseau is Latin avicellus, a little bird; Spanish keeps ave as the formal word beside pájaro (Latin passer, sparrow).
German Vogel is the cognate of English "fowl", the word "bird" replaced.
Chinese niǎo (simplified 鸟) and Japanese tori: a long-tailed bird, drawn in profile.

pages.title: Mother
pages.desc: PIE *méh₂tēr is intact from English to Hindi, and the "ma" syllable recurs far beyond Indo-European because it is one of the first sounds infants make. Several languages keep two words: a formal one and the one used at home.

facts.text: English: mother · Spanish: madre · French: mère · German: Mutter · Russian: мать matʹ · Hindi: माँ mā̃ · Arabic: أم ʾumm · Mandarin Chinese: 母亲 mǔqīn · Japanese: 母 haha · Korean: 어머니 eomeoni · Swahili: mama · Turkish: anne
English mother, German Mutter, Spanish madre, French mère, Russian мать and Hindi माँ (Sanskrit mātṛ).
Swahili mama, Chinese māma, Korean eomma and Arabic ʾumm are not cognates: "ma" words arise independently from babbling.
Chinese mǔ and Japanese haha (bō in compounds) share the character, a nursing figure.

pages.title: Father
pages.desc: PIE *ph₂tḗr gives father, Vater, padre, père and Hindi पिता. Russian chose the nursery word *atta instead (отец), and "baba" is the father in Swahili and Turkish, and in Chinese bàba, by the same babbling logic as mama.

facts.text: English: father · Spanish: padre · French: père · German: Vater · Russian: отец otéts · Hindi: पिता pitā · Arabic: أب ʾab · Mandarin Chinese: 父亲 fùqīn · Japanese: 父 chichi · Korean: 아버지 abeoji · Swahili: baba · Turkish: baba
English father, German Vater, Spanish padre, French père and Hindi पिता (Sanskrit pitṛ); Grimm’s law turned p into f in Germanic.
Swahili baba and Turkish baba are not related; both, like Chinese bàba and Arabic ʾab, are nursery words.

pages.title: Child
pages.desc: The child is "the one who cannot speak" in French (enfant, from Latin infans), a kin-word in German (Kind, from the root of kin and genus), and a nursery word in Spanish (niño). Swahili and Arabic mark the plural on the front and in the middle respectively.

facts.text: English: child · Spanish: niño · French: enfant · German: Kind · Russian: ребёнок rebyónok · Hindi: बच्चा baccā · Arabic: طفل ṭifl · Mandarin Chinese: 孩子 háizi · Japanese: 子供 kodomo · Korean: 아이 ai · Swahili: mtoto · Turkish: çocuk
French enfant, "not speaking"; English "infant" is the same word borrowed back.
German Kind shares its root with English kin, kind, king and Latin genus.

pages.title: Man
pages.desc: Hindi आदमी and Turkish adam are both Arabic Ādam: a man is a son of Adam. Chinese, Japanese and Korean share the character 男, "strength in the field". English "man" once meant any person; Spanish hombre and French homme come from Latin homo, human.

facts.text: English: man · Spanish: hombre · French: homme · German: Mann · Russian: мужчина mužčína · Hindi: आदमी ādmī · Arabic: رجل rajul · Mandarin Chinese: 男人 nánrén · Japanese: 男 otoko · Korean: 남자 namja · Swahili: mwanamume · Turkish: adam
Hindi आदमी and Turkish adam both borrowed the name of the first man as the ordinary word for a man.
Chinese nán, Japanese otoko (dan in compounds) and Korean namja (男子): 田 field over 力 strength.
English man and German Mann; Russian мужчина (from муж, husband) is a more distant relative.
Spanish hombre and French homme mean "human" by origin; the Latin word for a male was vir.

pages.title: Woman
pages.desc: Hindi औरत is Arabic ʿawra; Chinese, Japanese and Korean share the character 女; Russian женщина and English "queen" descend from the same PIE *gʷḗn. English woman was "wife-person", German Frau was "lady".

facts.text: English: woman · Spanish: mujer · French: femme · German: Frau · Russian: женщина žénščina · Hindi: औरत aurat · Arabic: امرأة imraʾa · Mandarin Chinese: 女人 nǚrén · Japanese: 女 onna · Korean: 여자 yeoja · Swahili: mwanamke · Turkish: kadın
Russian женщина (from жена, wife), Greek gynḗ (gynaecology) and English queen are one word.
Hindi औरत came through Persian from an Arabic word for what should be covered.
Chinese nǚ, Japanese onna and Korean yeoja (女子).
Spanish mujer and French femme took different Latin words; Latin femina is also "feminine".

pages.title: Heart
pages.desc: PIE *ḱḗr gives heart, Herz, corazón, cœur, сердце and Greek kardía (cardiac). Hindi took Persian dil, Turkish took Arabic qalb. In Chinese, Japanese and Korean the character 心 is heart and mind at once.

facts.text: English: heart · Spanish: corazón · French: cœur · German: Herz · Russian: сердце sérdtse · Hindi: दिल dil · Arabic: قلب qalb · Mandarin Chinese: 心 xīn · Japanese: 心 kokoro · Korean: 심장 simjang · Swahili: moyo · Turkish: kalp
English heart, German Herz, Spanish corazón, French cœur and Russian сердце; Sanskrit hṛdaya and Greek kardía too.
Hindi दिल is the Persian word, itself an Indo-European cousin of heart.
Turkish kalp is Arabic قلب.
Chinese xīn, Japanese kokoro and Korean simjang (心臟): the character is a drawing of the organ.

pages.title: Hand
pages.desc: Germanic *handuz (hand, Hand) against Latin manus (mano, main, manual). In Russian and Swahili the word covers the whole arm. The Chinese character 手 is a hand with spread fingers.

facts.text: English: hand · Spanish: mano · French: main · German: Hand · Russian: рука ruká · Hindi: हाथ hāth · Arabic: يد yad · Mandarin Chinese: 手 shǒu · Japanese: 手 te · Korean: 손 son · Swahili: mkono · Turkish: el
English hand and German Hand; no secure relatives outside Germanic.
Spanish mano and French main; English manual, manufacture, manuscript.
Chinese shǒu and Japanese te; as a radical it is squeezed to 扌 on the left of a character.

pages.title: Eye
pages.desc: PIE *h₃ekʷ- survives as eye, Auge, ojo, œil, Hindi आँख and Latin oculus; Russian replaced око with глаз. Arabic ʿayn is also a spring of water and a letter of the alphabet; Korean 눈 is also snow.

facts.text: English: eye · Spanish: ojo · French: œil · German: Auge · Russian: глаз glaz · Hindi: आँख ā̃kh · Arabic: عين ʿayn · Mandarin Chinese: 眼睛 yǎnjing · Japanese: 目 me · Korean: 눈 nun · Swahili: jicho · Turkish: göz
English eye, German Auge, Spanish ojo, French œil (Latin oculus) and Hindi आँख (Sanskrit akṣi); Russian’s poetic око too.

pages.title: Head
pages.desc: Latin caput (cabeza, capital) was replaced in French by testa, "pot", and in German by Kopf, from Latin cuppa, "cup": two languages independently calling the head a crock. Chinese and Japanese share 頭; Turkish baş is also "chief" and "beginning".

facts.text: English: head · Spanish: cabeza · French: tête · German: Kopf · Russian: голова golová · Hindi: सिर sir · Arabic: رأس raʾs · Mandarin Chinese: 头 tóu · Japanese: 頭 atama · Korean: 머리 meori · Swahili: kichwa · Turkish: baş
French tête (Latin testa) and German Kopf (Latin cuppa) are both slang that became standard; English "head" and German Haupt keep the old Germanic word.
Spanish cabeza, from capitia; English capital, captain and chapter are from the same root.
Chinese tóu (simplified 头) and Japanese atama.

pages.title: One
pages.desc: PIE *óynos: one, eins, uno, un, один, and with a different suffix Sanskrit eka, Hindi एक. Chinese, Japanese and Korean share the single stroke 一; Japanese and Korean both run two number series, native and Sinitic.

facts.text: English: one · Spanish: uno · French: un · German: eins · Russian: один odín · Hindi: एक ek · Arabic: واحد wāḥid · Mandarin Chinese: 一 yī · Japanese: 一 ichi · Korean: 하나 hana · Swahili: moja · Turkish: bir
English one, German eins, Spanish uno, French un and Russian один; Hindi एक (Sanskrit eka) uses the same root with another suffix.
Chinese yī, Japanese ichi and Korean il (일) in the Sino-Korean series; Korean 하나 and Japanese hitotsu are the native counts.

pages.title: Two
pages.desc: PIE *dwóh₁ is everywhere in Indo-European: two, zwei, dos, deux, два, Hindi दो, Latin duo. East Asia shares the two strokes of 二. Arabic adds a dual ending to nouns, so it rarely needs the word.

facts.text: English: two · Spanish: dos · French: deux · German: zwei · Russian: два dva · Hindi: दो do · Arabic: اثنان iṯnān · Mandarin Chinese: 二 èr · Japanese: 二 ni · Korean: 둘 dul · Swahili: mbili · Turkish: iki
English two (the w still sounds in twin and twelve), German zwei, Spanish dos, French deux, Russian два and Hindi दो (Sanskrit dvi).
Chinese èr, Japanese ni and Korean i (이) in the Sino-Korean series.

pages.title: Three
pages.desc: PIE *tréyes: three, drei, tres, trois, три, Hindi तीन. Three strokes make 三 in Chinese, Japanese and Sino-Korean. In Arabic, three to ten take the opposite gender of the noun they count.

facts.text: English: three · Spanish: tres · French: trois · German: drei · Russian: три tri · Hindi: तीन tīn · Arabic: ثلاثة ṯalāṯa · Mandarin Chinese: 三 sān · Japanese: 三 san · Korean: 셋 set · Swahili: tatu · Turkish: üç
English three, German drei, Spanish tres, French trois, Russian три and Hindi तीन (Sanskrit trīṇi).
Chinese sān, Japanese san and Korean sam (삼).

pages.title: Hello
pages.desc: Greetings are the newest words here and the most borrowed. English hello is a telephone-age word; Turkish merhaba is Arabic; Korean annyeong is Chinese "peace"; Japanese konnichiwa is half a sentence; Hindi namaste is a Sanskrit bow.

facts.text: English: hello · Spanish: hola · French: bonjour · German: hallo · Russian: здравствуйте zdrávstvuyte · Hindi: नमस्ते namaste · Arabic: مرحبا marḥaban · Mandarin Chinese: 你好 nǐ hǎo · Japanese: こんにちは konnichiwa · Korean: 안녕하세요 annyeonghaseyo · Swahili: jambo · Turkish: merhaba
Turkish merhaba is the Arabic greeting, "welcome, there is room for you".
Korean annyeonghaseyo asks "are you at peace?" with a Chinese-derived word for peace.
Hindi नमस्ते is "a bow to you".
English hello and German hallo are the same 19th-century exclamation, spread by the telephone.

pages.title: Thank you
pages.desc: Thanks is a thought (English thank, German danke), a grace (Spanish gracias), a reward (French merci), a prayer (Russian спасибо, "God save you") or a rarity (Japanese arigatō). Arabic šukr travelled to Hindi and Turkish; Chinese 感謝 is inside Korean gamsa.

facts.text: English: thank you · Spanish: gracias · French: merci · German: danke · Russian: спасибо spasíbo · Hindi: धन्यवाद dhanyavād · Arabic: شكرا šukran · Mandarin Chinese: 谢谢 xièxie · Japanese: ありがとう arigatō · Korean: 감사합니다 gamsahamnida · Swahili: asante · Turkish: teşekkür ederim
English thank and German danke, from the root of "think": gratitude as a thought.
Turkish teşekkür and Hindi śukriyā (beside धन्यवाद) are from the Arabic root š-k-r.
Spanish gracias is "graces"; French merci is "wages, reward".
Korean gamsahamnida carries the Chinese compound 感謝; Chinese xièxie doubles its second character.
Arigatō is from an adjective meaning "difficult to exist", hence rare and precious.

pages.title: Yes
pages.desc: Yes is surprisingly unstable. Spanish sí is Latin sic, "thus"; French oui is hoc ille, "this is it", and gave the langue d’oïl its name; Chinese has no single word and repeats the verb instead; Japanese hai means "I hear you".

facts.text: English: yes · Spanish: sí · French: oui · German: ja · Russian: да da · Hindi: हाँ hā̃ · Arabic: نعم naʿam · Mandarin Chinese: 是 shì · Japanese: はい hai · Korean: 네 ne · Swahili: ndiyo · Turkish: evet
Spanish sí from sic; French oui from hoc ille, while French si (from sic) survives to contradict a negative.

pages.title: No
pages.desc: Negation is older and steadier than affirmation: PIE *ne is inside English no, German nein, Latin non (Spanish no, French non), Russian нет, Hindi नहीं and Sanskrit na. Turkish hayır is, by origin, the Arabic word for "good".

facts.text: English: no · Spanish: no · French: non · German: nein · Russian: нет nyet · Hindi: नहीं nahī̃ · Arabic: لا lā · Mandarin Chinese: 不 bù · Japanese: いいえ iie · Korean: 아니요 aniyo · Swahili: hapana · Turkish: hayır
Spanish no and French non.
German nein is "not one"; English no is "not ever"; Russian нет is "there is not".

pages.title: Friend
pages.desc: A friend is a lover in Germanic (friend and free share a root), in Latin (amicus, from amare) and in Persian (dōst, which Hindi and Turkish both borrowed). Swahili rafiki is Arabic "companion"; Turkish arkadaş is "back-fellow", one who has your back.

facts.text: English: friend · Spanish: amigo · French: ami · German: Freund · Russian: друг drug · Hindi: दोस्त dost · Arabic: صديق ṣadīq · Mandarin Chinese: 朋友 péngyou · Japanese: 友達 tomodachi · Korean: 친구 chingu · Swahili: rafiki · Turkish: arkadaş
English friend and German Freund, "the loving one", from the root of "free".
Spanish amigo and French ami, from amare, to love.
Hindi दोस्त and Turkish dost (beside arkadaş) are the same Persian word.
Swahili rafiki is Arabic رفيق, companion.
Korean chingu is a Chinese compound, "close and old".

pages.title: World
pages.desc: Arabic dunyā became the word for the world in Hindi, Swahili and Turkish; Chinese 世界, a Buddhist coinage, became Japanese sekai and Korean segye. English world and German Welt are "the age of man"; Russian мир is also "peace".

facts.text: English: world · Spanish: mundo · French: monde · German: Welt · Russian: мир mir · Hindi: दुनिया duniyā · Arabic: عالم ʿālam · Mandarin Chinese: 世界 shìjiè · Japanese: 世界 sekai · Korean: 세계 segye · Swahili: dunia · Turkish: dünya
Hindi दुनिया, Swahili dunia and Turkish dünya: one Arabic loan in three unrelated families.
Chinese shìjiè, Japanese sekai and Korean segye, a compound coined to translate Buddhist Sanskrit.
English world and German Welt: wer "man" + ald "age".
Spanish mundo and French monde; Latin mundus also meant clean and elegant, a calque of Greek kosmos.

pages.title: Day
pages.desc: A false friend at the top: English day and Latin dies look alike but are unrelated. Dies (Spanish día, French jour via diurnum), Russian день and Hindi दिन come from PIE *dyew-, "to shine", the root of Zeus and Jupiter. Japanese and Chinese write day with the sun character 日.

facts.text: English: day · Spanish: día · French: jour · German: Tag · Russian: день denʹ · Hindi: दिन din · Arabic: يوم yawm · Mandarin Chinese: 天 tiān · Japanese: 日 hi · Korean: 날 nal · Swahili: siku · Turkish: gün
Latin dies (Spanish día, French jour), Russian день and Sanskrit dina (Hindi दिन) share the root of Zeus, Jupiter and "deity".
English day and German Tag: not from dies, despite appearances.
Japanese hi, Korean il (일) and Chinese rì all use the sun character for the day.

pages.title: Night
pages.desc: PIE *nókʷts is almost as well preserved as star: night, Nacht, noche, nuit, ночь, Latin nox. Hindi रात is Sanskrit rātri instead. Swahili builds night from day: u-siku. Korean 밤 is also "chestnut", differing only in vowel length.

facts.text: English: night · Spanish: noche · French: nuit · German: Nacht · Russian: ночь nočʹ · Hindi: रात rāt · Arabic: ليل layl · Mandarin Chinese: 夜晚 yèwǎn · Japanese: 夜 yoru · Korean: 밤 bam · Swahili: usiku · Turkish: gece
English night, German Nacht, Spanish noche, French nuit and Russian ночь (Latin nox, Greek nýx).
Hindi रात took the other Sanskrit word for night.
Chinese yè and Japanese yoru.
Night is derived from the word for day with the u- prefix.

pages.title: Five ways to write
pages.desc: Writing systems differ in what a sign stands for. An alphabet writes consonants and vowels (Latin, Cyrillic, Hangul); an abjad writes mainly consonants (Arabic); an abugida writes a consonant with an inherent vowel that marks modify (Devanagari); a syllabary writes whole syllables (kana); a logography writes morphemes (Chinese characters).

facts.text: Latin for six languages, then Cyrillic, Devanagari, Arabic, Han characters, kana (with kanji) and Hangul.
Letters write phonemes, kana write syllables (morae), characters write morphemes: each system picks a rung of the ladder to make visible.

pages.title: Latin script
pages.desc: The alphabet of the Romans, itself from Etruscan and Greek, now writes more languages than any other. Six of the twelve brains use it, each with its own additions: Spanish ñ, French ç and œ, German ä ö ü ß, Turkish ğ ı ş, Swahili with none.

facts.text: English, Spanish, French, German, Swahili and Turkish; Turkish adopted it in 1928 and Swahili in the nineteenth century, both replacing Arabic script.
The ISO basic alphabet has 26 letters; English squeezes about 44 phonemes into them, which is why its spelling is hard, while Spanish, Swahili and Turkish spell almost one sound per letter.

pages.title: Cyrillic
pages.desc: Devised in the First Bulgarian Empire in the ninth century from Greek uncial letters, with new signs for Slavic sounds (ж, ш, ч, ю). Russian uses 33 letters; some fifty languages from Serbian to Mongolian and Kazakh have used the script.

facts.text: Named for Saint Cyril, though his own invention was the earlier Glagolitic script; Cyrillic’s а в г д are plainly Greek α β γ δ.
Peter the Great’s 1708 civil script simplified the letterforms; the 1918 Soviet reform dropped four letters, giving the modern Russian alphabet.

pages.title: Devanagari
pages.desc: An abugida: each consonant sign carries an inherent a, and vowel marks above, below or beside it change the vowel. Letters hang from a headline that joins each word. Used for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit.

facts.text: Devanagari descends from Brahmi (third century BCE), the ancestor of nearly every script of South and Southeast Asia, from Tibetan to Thai.
The alphabet runs from the back of the mouth forward (क ख ग घ ङ …) in rows by place of articulation: a phonetic classification two thousand years old.

pages.title: Arabic script
pages.desc: An abjad written right to left: 28 letters write consonants and long vowels, short vowels are optional marks, and most letters change shape depending on their position in the word. It is the second most used script in the world.

facts.text: Persian, Urdu, Pashto and Uyghur use it with extra letters; Ottoman Turkish and coastal Swahili (Ajami) were written in it before switching to Latin.
Because short vowels are usually unwritten, the three-consonant root of a word stands out on the page: كتب is k-t-b whatever vowels are read into it.

pages.title: Chinese characters
pages.desc: The oldest writing system still in use: oracle-bone inscriptions from about 1200 BCE are legible ancestors of today’s characters. Each character writes a syllable and a morpheme; about 3,000 cover everyday reading, and a large dictionary lists over 50,000.

facts.text: 水 water, 火 fire, 日 sun, 月 moon, 雨 rain and 木 tree began as drawings; most characters combine a meaning radical with a sound component.
Japan writes with them as kanji, Korea used them as hanja (now rare), Vietnam as chữ Nôm until the twentieth century: the same character read in different languages.
The People’s Republic simplified many characters in the 1950s and 60s: 魚 became 鱼, 鳥 became 鸟, 頭 became 头; Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan keep the older forms.

pages.title: Kana (with kanji)
pages.desc: Japanese is written with three scripts at once: kanji (Chinese characters) for word roots, hiragana for grammar and native words, katakana for loanwords and emphasis. The two kana are syllabaries of 46 basic signs each, derived from cursive and fragmentary kanji in the Heian period.

facts.text: 水を飲みます (I drink water) uses kanji for water and the verb root and hiragana for the particle and ending; コーヒー (coffee) is katakana.
Each kana writes one mora, a unit of timing: Tokyo is four morae (to-u-kyo-u), and haiku count morae, not syllables.

pages.title: Hangul
pages.desc: Promulgated by King Sejong in 1446 as Hunminjeongeum, "the correct sounds for the instruction of the people". Its consonant letters depict the mouth making them (ㄱ the tongue root, ㅁ the lips, ㅅ a tooth) and letters are stacked into syllable blocks: 물 is m-u-l in one square.

facts.text: Adding a stroke adds a feature: ㄱ g, ㅋ k (aspirated), ㄲ kk (tense). No other national script encodes phonetic features in letter shape.
Sejong’s preface says a wise man can learn it in a morning; Korea’s near-total literacy and Hangul Day (9 October) honour the design.

pages.title: The International Phonetic Alphabet
pages.desc: One symbol for every speech sound, so that any word in any language can be written the same way. Devised in 1888 and revised since, it is the script linguists use to compare the brains in this network.

facts.text: English "thank" is /θæŋk/, German "danke" /ˈdaŋkə/, and the IPA shows what the spellings hide: the same final cluster, different first consonant.

pages.title: Proto-Indo-European
pages.desc: The reconstructed ancestor of English, Spanish, French, German, Russian and Hindi, spoken perhaps 4500–2500 BCE, most likely on the Pontic–Caspian steppe. Never written: every form, like *wódr̥ for water, is inferred from its descendants by regular sound correspondences, which is why they carry an asterisk.

facts.text: The comparative method lines up water, Wasser, вода and Hittite watar and works backwards to the sounds that could have produced all of them.
Archaeology and ancient DNA point to the Yamnaya culture north of the Black Sea as the most likely speakers, spreading with wheeled vehicles and horses.
Star, night, three, mother, father, sun and heart survive in all six Indo-European brains here.

pages.title: Indo-European
pages.desc: The largest family by speakers: about 3.4 billion people, nearly half of humanity, from Iceland to Bangladesh. Six of the twelve brains belong to it, in four branches: Germanic (English, German), Romance (Spanish, French), Slavic (Russian) and Indo-Aryan (Hindi).

facts.text: Germanic, Romance (the daughters of Latin), Balto-Slavic and Indo-Iranian; Celtic, Greek, Armenian, Albanian and the extinct Anatolian and Tocharian complete the family.
Noticing that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin shared "a stronger affinity than could possibly have been produced by accident", Jones proposed a common source: the founding moment of historical linguistics.

pages.title: Germanic
pages.desc: English and German, with Dutch, the Scandinavian languages and Afrikaans: about 500 million native speakers. Marked by Grimm’s law (p, t, k became f, þ, h) and stress fixed on the first syllable.

facts.text: Latin pāter, piscis, cor against father, fish, heart: the consonant shift that defines the branch, formulated by Jacob Grimm of the fairy tales in 1822.
German moved its consonants a second time (water/Wasser, two/zwei, apple/Apfel), which is why German and English differ more than German and Dutch.

pages.title: Romance
pages.desc: The daughters of spoken Latin: Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Romanian and about forty smaller languages, some 900 million speakers. Not from Cicero’s Latin but from the Vulgar Latin of soldiers and settlers.

facts.text: Spanish and French come from the everyday Latin of the provinces, which preferred caballus to equus (horse) and focus to ignis (fire).
aqua: agua, eau · noctem: noche, nuit · caput: cabeza, chef · French has eroded further than Spanish in almost every word.

pages.title: Slavic
pages.desc: Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Czech, Serbo-Croatian, Bulgarian and others: about 315 million speakers across Eastern Europe. Noted for its case systems, verbal aspect and the Cyrillic script in its eastern and southern branches.

facts.text: Proto-Slavic was still one language around 500 CE; Russian, Polish and Bulgarian remain partly mutually intelligible in basic vocabulary (voda, woda, voda).

pages.title: Indo-Aryan
pages.desc: Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Punjabi, Marathi, Gujarati and hundreds more, descended from Sanskrit and its Prakrits: about 800 million native speakers across South Asia.

facts.text: Sanskrit trīṇi, sūrya, mātṛ, pitṛ became Hindi तीन, सूरज, माँ, पिता; the Vedas, around 1500 BCE, are the oldest Indo-European texts after Hittite.

pages.title: Afro-Asiatic
pages.desc: Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, Berber, Somali, Hausa and ancient Egyptian: about 500 million speakers across North Africa and the Middle East, and the family with the longest written record, from Egyptian hieroglyphs and Akkadian cuneiform.

facts.text: Arabic’s branch, with Hebrew, Aramaic, Amharic and the extinct Akkadian and Phoenician; the Phoenician alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Cyrillic and Arabic script alike.

pages.title: Semitic
pages.desc: Arabic, Hebrew, Aramaic and the Ethiopian Semitic languages. The signature is the consonantal root: three consonants carry the meaning and vowel patterns carry the grammar.

facts.text: k-t-b gives kataba (he wrote), kitāb (book), kātib (writer), maktab (office); Hebrew k-t-v does the same.

pages.title: Sino-Tibetan
pages.desc: The Chinese languages (Mandarin, Cantonese, Wu, Min and others) together with Tibetan and Burmese: about 1.4 billion speakers, the second-largest family. Mandarin is its giant.

facts.text: The Chinese "dialects" are as different as the Romance languages but share one written standard, which is why a Cantonese and a Mandarin speaker can read the same newspaper and not understand each other aloud.

pages.title: Japonic
pages.desc: Japanese and the Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa: a small family with no proven relatives, though Japanese has borrowed half its vocabulary from Chinese.

facts.text: The languages of the Ryukyu islands split from mainland Japanese well over a thousand years ago and are not mutually intelligible with it; most are now endangered.

pages.title: Koreanic
pages.desc: Korean and Jeju, the language of Jeju Island: another small family of its own. Like Japanese it is verb-final, agglutinative and layered with Chinese loanwords, but no genetic link between the two has been demonstrated.

facts.text: Spoken on Jeju Island and classified by UNESCO as critically endangered, Jeju is distinct enough from Seoul Korean to count as a separate language.

pages.title: The Altaic question
pages.desc: For a century linguists proposed an Altaic family uniting Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic, often with Korean and Japanese. Most now reject it: the shared features (verb-final order, vowel harmony, suffixes, no gender) are explained by contact and typology, not common descent.

facts.text: Turkish, Korean and Japanese all put the verb last and stack suffixes, yet their core vocabularies, the words in this brain, show no regular correspondences.

pages.title: Niger–Congo
pages.desc: The largest family by number of languages, around 1,500, spoken across sub-Saharan Africa: Yoruba, Igbo, Fula, Shona, Zulu and the whole Bantu group including Swahili.

facts.text: Some 500 languages that spread from the Nigeria–Cameroon border across central, eastern and southern Africa in the last 3,000 years, the Bantu expansion.

pages.title: Bantu
pages.desc: Swahili, Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Kikuyu, Lingala and hundreds more. The name means "people" (ba-ntu) and the signature is the noun class: every noun belongs to a class marked by a prefix that echoes through the sentence.

facts.text: Swahili mtoto/watoto (child/children) and mti/miti (tree/trees) switch prefix for plural, and adjectives and verbs copy the prefix.

pages.title: Turkic
pages.desc: Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur, Tatar and others: about 200 million speakers from the Balkans to Siberia. The family spread west from Mongolia and the Altai with nomadic empires from the sixth century on.

facts.text: A Turkish speaker can follow much Azerbaijani and some Turkmen; the eastern languages are more distant but share the core words: su (water), bir, iki, üç.

pages.title: Isolates and the unclassified
pages.desc: Basque, Korean (if Jeju is counted a dialect), Ainu, Burushaski and over a hundred other languages have no demonstrable relatives. Their existence is a reminder that most of the family tree is lost.

facts.text: Spoken in the Pyrenees since before Latin arrived, Basque is the only pre-Indo-European language of Western Europe to survive.

pages.title: Utterance · what someone says
pages.desc: The largest unit: a stretch of speech by one speaker, bounded by silence. Discourse analysis works here, with turns, topics and the way "hello" opens a conversation and "thank you" closes it. Below this rung the units become grammatical.

facts.text: Greetings and thanks are utterances whose whole meaning is social: they manage the conversation rather than describe the world.

pages.title: Sentence · words in order
pages.desc: A unit with a subject and a predicate. Languages differ most visibly in where they put the verb: English, Spanish, French, Chinese and Swahili say "the dog sees the fish" (SVO); Hindi, Japanese, Korean and Turkish say "the dog the fish sees" (SOV); Classical Arabic begins with the verb.

facts.text: SOV is the most common order among the world’s languages, SVO second; together they cover about 85%. German puts the verb second in main clauses and last in subordinate ones.

pages.title: Word · the unit we name
pages.desc: A free-standing unit of meaning, yet hard to define: Chinese writes without spaces, Turkish stacks a whole clause into one word (evlerimizden, "from our houses"), and English cannot decide whether "ice cream" is one word or two.

facts.text: Spaces between words are a medieval European invention; Latin, Greek and Chinese were written in unbroken runs, and Japanese and Chinese still are.
The 360 word satellites in this network are the atoms of its twelve brains; each one is a label for a shared meaning and a node in a history of borrowing and inheritance.

pages.title: Morpheme · the smallest piece of meaning
pages.desc: The smallest unit that means something: un-, friend, -ly in "unfriendly". Arabic hides its morphemes inside the word as consonant roots and vowel patterns; Swahili puts them in front as prefixes; Turkish lines them up behind as suffixes; Chinese writes one per character.

facts.lead: Four ways to build a word
facts.text: Root-and-pattern (Arabic k-t-b), prefixing (Swahili wa-toto), suffixing (Turkish ev-ler-imiz-den) and isolating (Chinese 朋友, two morphemes, two characters).
Korean 물고기 (water-meat, fish), Swahili mwanamke (person-wife, woman), English woman (wife-person): morphemes fused into new words.

pages.title: Syllable · the beat
pages.desc: A vowel with consonants around it: the unit of rhythm, poetry and, in Japanese, Korean and Chinese, of writing. Chinese characters are one syllable each; Hangul stacks letters into syllable blocks; kana write one mora apiece.

facts.text: Hangul 물, kana みず (mi-zu) and the character 水 all make the syllable visible; alphabets hide it.
Japanese allows little more than consonant+vowel, so "Christmas" becomes ku-ri-su-ma-su (five syllables); English allows "strengths", one syllable with eight consonant sounds.

pages.title: Phoneme · the smallest sound that changes meaning
pages.desc: A unit of sound that distinguishes words: English pin and bin differ in one phoneme. Languages have between about 11 (Rotokas) and over 100 (Taa); English has around 44, Spanish 24, Hawaiian 13. In Mandarin, tone is phonemic: mā, má, mǎ and mà are four words.

facts.text: Korean 눈 (eye) and 눈 (snow), 밤 (night) and 밤 (chestnut) differ only in vowel length: length is a phoneme in Korean but not in English.
Inventories range from about a dozen to over a hundred; the IPA has a symbol for each.

pages.title: Distinctive feature · what a sound is made of
pages.desc: Each phoneme is a bundle of binary features: voiced or not, nasal or not, where the tongue is, how much the airflow is blocked. /p/ and /b/ differ in exactly one, voicing. This is the atom of phonology, and Hangul is the only widely used script that writes it.

facts.text: ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ (g, k, kk) add a stroke per feature; Devanagari’s row-by-row order groups letters by place and manner.

pages.title: Grapheme · the written atom
pages.desc: The smallest unit of a writing system: a letter, a kana sign, a character. What it stands for depends on the system: a Latin letter writes (roughly) a phoneme, a kana writes a mora, a Chinese character writes a morpheme and a syllable at once, and a Hangul letter writes a phoneme but is arranged by syllable.

facts.text: Writing is a second ladder laid beside speech: alphabets attach at the phoneme, syllabaries at the syllable, logographies at the morpheme.

pages.title: Sound · the physics underneath
pages.desc: Below the feature there is no more language, only air: a pressure wave shaped by the vocal tract, whose resonances (formants) carry the vowel and whose bursts and hisses carry the consonants. For what the air itself is made of, open the Atomic brain.

facts.text: The vowel in "water" is a pattern of resonant peaks, F1 and F2, set by tongue height and backness; a spectrogram shows them as dark bands.
Air is nitrogen and oxygen molecules; molecules are atoms; atoms are electron clouds around nuclei. The Atomic brain continues the ladder from a nanometre to the Planck length.

pages.title: English · English
pages.desc: The most spoken language on Earth is a West Germanic language from the North Sea coast that borrowed most of its dictionary from French and Latin. Its grammar has shed gender and almost all case; its spelling preserves sounds that vanished five centuries ago.

facts.text: Only 372 million learned it first: English is the world’s most-used second language, and the lingua franca of science, aviation and the internet.
The hundred commonest words and the grammar are Germanic; after the Norman Conquest of 1066 English took in tens of thousands of French and Latin words, so most of its dictionary is Romance.

facts.lead: Spelling frozen before the sounds moved
facts.text: The Great Vowel Shift (c. 1400–1700) changed every long vowel after printing had fixed the spellings: moon, one and eye are written as Chaucer said them.
Old English had three genders and five cases; modern English keeps gender only in pronouns and case only in the possessive, and relies on subject–verb–object order.
English’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Spanish · español
pages.desc: The Vulgar Latin of the Iberian Peninsula, carried to the Americas after 1492 and now the second-largest native-speaker community in the world. Nearly phonemic spelling, two genders, and about four thousand words left by eight centuries of Arabic al-Andalus.

facts.text: 487 million native speakers across Spain and twenty countries of the Americas; the United States has the second-largest Spanish-speaking population after Mexico.
agua from aqua, noche from noctem, ojo from oculum: regular sound changes turned Latin into Castilian, and Arabic added almohada, aceite, ojalá and some 4,000 more words.
Every noun is masculine or feminine; agua is feminine but takes el before its stressed a-, mano is feminine despite -o and día masculine despite -a.
Five pure vowels and a spelling so regular that dictation is rarely a school subject; ñ, from a doubled n, is its signature letter.
Spanish’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: French · français
pages.desc: The Latin of Gaul, worn smooth: silent final consonants, nasal vowels and a spelling that records a pronunciation centuries old. The language of diplomacy for three hundred years, now spoken by more people in Africa than in Europe.

facts.text: 75 million native speakers; the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie counts over 320 million francophones, the majority of them in Africa.
aqua became eau, pronounced /o/; oculus became œil; the written final letters of petit, grand and trois fell silent, so French spelling preserves what the mouth dropped.
Latin’s neuter merged into the masculine; every noun is le or la, and adjectives and past participles agree.
quatre-vingts (four twenties) for 80 and soixante-dix (sixty-ten) for 70 are vigesimal survivals; Belgian and Swiss French say septante and nonante.
French’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: German · Deutsch
pages.desc: English’s closest big cousin, shifted twice: by Grimm’s law with the rest of Germanic, then by the High German consonant shift that made water into Wasser and two into zwei. Three genders, four cases, capitalised nouns and compounds of any length.

facts.text: 76 million native speakers, the largest first-language community in the European Union, across Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and South Tyrol.
The High German consonant shift turned t into z or s (two/zwei, water/Wasser), p into pf or f (apple/Apfel, ship/Schiff) and k into ch (make/machen).
der, die, das; nominative, accusative, dative, genitive; every noun capitalised. Gender is often arbitrary: das Mädchen (girl) is neuter because -chen is.
German writes compounds as one word: Sonnenlicht (sunlight), Mondschein (moonshine), Handschuh (hand-shoe, glove), Feuerwehr (fire-defence, fire brigade).
German’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Russian · русский
pages.desc: The largest Slavic language and the lingua franca of the former Soviet Union, written in Cyrillic. Six cases, three genders, free word order and verbs that come in pairs, one for the process and one for the result.

facts.text: 133 million native speakers in Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and beyond; one of the six official languages of the United Nations.
Descended from the ninth-century Bulgarian script modelled on Greek, reformed by Peter the Great and again in 1918.
вода becomes воду, воды, воде, водой as its role in the sentence changes; gender is readable from the ending, so мужчина (man) is a famous exception.
Nearly every verb has an imperfective form for the ongoing action and a perfective for its completion, a distinction English spreads across its tenses.
Russian’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Hindi · हिन्दी
pages.desc: The Sanskrit-descended language of the Gangetic plain, written in Devanagari, with a street vocabulary full of Persian and Arabic. With Urdu, its twin in Perso-Arabic script, it forms Hindustani, the common speech of some 800 million people.

facts.text: 347 million native speakers; Hindi and Urdu share grammar and everyday words and differ mainly in script and learned vocabulary.
An abugida: each consonant carries an inherent a, vowel signs hang from it, and a headline joins the letters of a word.

facts.lead: Sanskrit at the root, Persian in the street
facts.text: तीन, सूरज and माँ descend from Sanskrit; दिल, दोस्त, दुनिया and आदमी came through Persian during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal centuries.
Subject–object–verb, with postpositions (पानी में, "in water"); two genders, and verbs agree with the subject’s gender and number.
Hindi’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Arabic · العربية
pages.desc: Modern Standard Arabic is a learned standard, the language of writing, news and the Qurʾan across more than twenty countries, while daily life runs in regional varieties as different as the Romance languages. Written right to left in an abjad; built from three-consonant roots.

facts.text: Ethnologue counts no first-language speakers of the standard: children grow up with Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf or Maghrebi Arabic and learn the standard at school, a textbook case of diglossia.
Twenty-eight letters write consonants and long vowels; short vowels are optional marks; most letters take different shapes at the start, middle and end of a word.
Meaning lives in the root and grammar in the vowels: ʿ-l-m gives ʿālam (world), ʿilm (knowledge) and muʿallim (teacher); ṣ-d-q gives ṣadīq (friend) and ṣidq (truth).
With Islam and Indian Ocean trade, Arabic words settled in Swahili, Hindi, Turkish, Persian and Spanish: dunyā, qalb, rafīq, marḥaban, samak, and in Spanish about 4,000 more.
Arabic’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Mandarin Chinese · 普通话
pages.desc: Standard Chinese, Putonghua, based on the Beijing dialect: the language with the most native speakers, written in the oldest script still in use. Four tones, no inflection at all, and a measure word between every number and its noun.

facts.text: 988 million native speakers; Mandarin is one of several Chinese languages (Cantonese, Wu, Min, Hakka) that share a writing system but are not mutually intelligible when spoken.
mā 妈 (mother), má 麻 (hemp), mǎ 马 (horse), mà 骂 (scold): pitch contour is part of the word, and a neutral fifth tone appears in unstressed syllables like the second half of 谢谢.
Each character writes one syllable and one morpheme; about 3,000 cover a newspaper. 水, 火, 日, 月 began as pictures and are read in Japanese too.
Nouns and verbs never change form; time and number come from context and particles; counting needs a measure word: 一条鱼 (one fish), 一只鸟 (one bird), 两个人 (two people).
Mandarin Chinese’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Japanese · 日本語
pages.desc: Spoken by almost everyone in Japan and almost no one elsewhere, Japanese is a family nearly to itself. It writes with three scripts at once, puts the verb last, builds politeness into its verb endings and took half its vocabulary from Chinese.

facts.text: Japonic’s only relatives are the Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa; a kinship with Korean has been proposed for a century and never established.
Kanji for roots, hiragana for grammar, katakana for loanwords: 水 is read mizu as a native word and sui in Chinese-derived compounds.
Subject–object–verb; wa, ga, o and ni follow the noun to mark its role; politeness is grammatical, so arigatō and arigatō gozaimasu are different registers of one word.
About half the dictionary is Chinese-derived: 太陽 taiyō (sun), 世界 sekai (world); native words like tsuki and hoshi stand beside them.
Japanese’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Korean · 한국어
pages.desc: The language of both Koreas and a large diaspora, written in Hangul, the alphabet King Sejong designed in 1443. Verb-final and agglutinative, with two parallel number systems and verb endings that change with the listener’s status.

facts.text: Koreanic’s only other member is Jeju; large Korean-speaking communities live in China, the United States and Japan.
Consonant letters are shaped after the mouth that makes them and stacked with vowels into syllable blocks: 물 is m-u-l in one square.
Native 하나, 둘, 셋 for counting objects and ages; Sino-Korean 일, 이, 삼 for dates, money and minutes; both in daily use.
Verb endings encode the relationship: 감사합니다 to a stranger or elder, 고마워 to a friend; Sino-Korean words (친구, 세계) make up over half the vocabulary.
Korean’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Swahili · Kiswahili
pages.desc: A Bantu language of the East African coast whose name is Arabic for "of the coasts". Few people grow up speaking it, but it is the lingua franca of Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and the eastern Congo, and a working language of the African Union.

facts.text: The archetypal lingua franca: Swahili spread through trade, then through schooling and nation-building in Tanzania and Kenya.
Centuries of Indian Ocean trade left perhaps a sixth of the lexicon Arabic: rafiki, dunia, samaki, and the name Swahili itself from sawāḥil, coasts.
Nouns fall into classes marked by prefixes: m-/wa- for people (mtoto, watoto), m-/mi- for trees (mti, miti), ki-/vi- for things (kichwa, vichwa); adjectives and verbs copy the prefix.
Coastal Swahili was written in Arabic letters (Ajami) from at least the 1700s; a Latin orthography based on the Zanzibar dialect was standardised in the 1920s and 30s.
Swahili’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Turkish · Türkçe
pages.desc: The largest Turkic language, remade in the twentieth century: a Latin alphabet in 1928, then a purge of Arabic and Persian words. Vowel harmony runs through every suffix, and suffixes are how Turkish says almost everything.

facts.text: 86 million native speakers, mostly in Türkiye and Cyprus, with several million in Germany and across Europe.
Atatürk replaced Ottoman Arabic script with a 29-letter Latin alphabet (ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş, ü) in a matter of months; literacy rose steeply.
Agglutinative: ev-ler-imiz-den, "from our houses", is one word; each suffix vowel matches the root, so gün-ler but ay-lar.

facts.lead: Arabic and Persian layers, then purged
facts.text: Ottoman Turkish borrowed heavily; kalp, dünya, merhaba and teşekkür survive, but the language reform replaced thousands of loans with Turkic coinages.
Turkish’s words for the thirty shared meanings, grouped as nature, living things, people, the body, counting, everyday words, world & time.

pages.title: Reports are not verification
pages.desc: A statement, a social post, or a large audience can point at a claim without establishing it.

facts.text: Kelly defines verification as the limiting case of confirmation, the case in which evidence conclusively establishes a hypothesis, and says whether that case ever occurs is controversial.
